p: Venetus leaves out "godly" in the book's opening thesis.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints and Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ); Swete's footnote names only Venetus as differing
Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes

why: Two of the three codices have the adjective, and the thesis phrase recurs with it later (6:31; 13:1; 18:2), so the Plain English Translation keeps it. A copyist could easily drop a word in a long opening sentence.

p: Venetus changes the opening words, so that the verse no longer begins a condition.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints; Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes
Codex Venetus, first hand (V*), from Swete's footnotes
Codex Venetus, a later hand (Vᵃ), from Swete's footnotes

why: Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus agree, and "if, then" fits the argument of 1:3-4, which runs as a condition and its result ("it is also seen to be lord"). The Venetus readings break that link.

t: Be lord over, or hold back?
p: Venetus says reason "holds back" the passions that block justice, instead of "is lord over" them.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints and Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)
Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes

why: The thesis is about rule, and the verb matches the run of words for mastery in 1:1-7. Venetus's word may come from the words for hindering (kōlytikos, empodistikos) in 1:3-4.

p: Sinaiticus and Venetus leave out "and good sense", so only three virtues are named here.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints
readings.en: and self-restraint and good sense, opposing

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes

why: The base text is followed. The speech names four virtues in 1:2-4 and 1:18, so the full list fits its plan; but two codices against one is not weak support, and a copyist could as easily have added the fourth virtue to complete the list as dropped it.

p: Sinaiticus and Venetus both leave out "godly" here.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes (Venetus also puts "master", δεσπότης, before "sovereign")

why: Swete prints Alexandrinus. The reading without the adjective has two codices, and it is the shorter text; but the same two codices are not always independent, and the phrase "godly reason" is the book's own formula. The Plain English Translation follows the base text; the meaning of the thesis does not change.

p: Venetus calls the seven brothers "boys" instead of "men".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints and Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)
Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes

why: The book calls the brothers both "young men" and "children" elsewhere; here Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus agree, and the praise of their courage suits "men".

t: At this season, or at that time?
p: Venetus reads "at that time", which would remove the hint that the speech was given on a day of remembrance.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints and Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)
Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes

why: Two codices against one, and "this" is the harder reading, since a copyist who did not know the setting might change it to "that" to refer to the time of the martyrs.
b: See the note at 1:10 on the occasion of the speech.

a: together with a right way of life, puts the word of wisdom first
p: Sinaiticus and Venetus define reason with "right reason" (orthos logos), the Stoics' phrase, and "the life of wisdom".

readings.w: Swete's text: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints, which in fact has the slip ὀρθούς, corrected by Swete to ὀρθοῦ
readings.orig: μετὰ ὀρθοῦ βίου προτιμῶν τὸν σοφίας λόγον
readings.en: with right life preferring the word of wisdom
readings.plain: together with a right way of life, puts the word of wisdom first

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes
readings.orig: μετὰ ὀρθοῦ λόγου προτιμῶν τὸν σοφίας βίον
readings.en: with right reason preferring the life of wisdom
readings.plain: together with right reason, puts the life of wisdom first

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes
readings.orig: μετὰ ὀρθοῦ λόγου προτιμῶν τὸν σοφὸν βίον
readings.en: with right reason preferring the wise life
readings.plain: together with right reason, puts the wise life first

why: Swete's printed text is a mixture: the words of Alexandrinus, with Swete's correction of its slip ὀρθούς to ὀρθοῦ. Sinaiticus and Venetus agree on "right reason" (ὀρθοῦ λόγου) and differ only in the last words. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text, the base text of this site, but the reading of the other two codices is a strong rival, and Swete's notes do not settle which is older.
b: The Stoics spoke of "the right reason pervading everything", which they identified with Zeus. A definition of human reasoning as "mind with right reason" would put the book's thesis in those terms; Alexandrinus's "right life" ties it instead to living by the law (1:17).

a: eating anything at all, gorging, and eating alone
t: The bodily vices: order and number
p: The three codices differ in the list: Sinaiticus reverses the last two, Venetus lacks "gorging".

readings.w: Swete's text (Alexandrinus, with Swete's correction of its slip νομοφαγία)
readings.en: eating anything, gorging and eating alone
readings.plain: eating anything at all, gorging, and eating alone

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes
readings.en: eating anything, eating alone and gorging
readings.plain: eating anything at all, eating alone, and gorging

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes
readings.plain: eating anything at all and eating alone

why: The base text is followed. All three codices have "eating anything" and "eating alone"; Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus both have "gorging" too, only in a different place, so Venetus's shorter list looks like an omission.
b: See the note on "eating alone" for Alexandrinus's slip nomophagia.

p: Alexandrinus has a word that makes little sense here; the Plain English Translation follows Sinaiticus and Venetus.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes (spelled φειμοῦται); Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Brenton's English ("reined in")
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints
readings.en: strive for honor, are made ambitious

why: This is a departure from the base text. "All the urges of the body are made to strive for honor by reason" hardly fits the sentence, while "muzzled" matches "resisted and bent back" just before. The two words differ by only a few letters (φιμουνται / φιλοτιμουνται), so Alexandrinus's reading is most likely a slip. In the same verse the Plain English Translation follows Swete's text for the first two verbs (see the variants on "resisted" and "bent back"), so only this clause follows Sinaiticus and Venetus.

p: Sinaiticus has a verb that means "held back, checked" for Alexandrinus's "resisted".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints
readings.en: are resisted, are held out against

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes

why: The base text is followed. The lexicon of Liddell and Scott gives "hold out against, withstand" for ἀντέχω, and quotes Sinaiticus's reading at this verse under ἀνέχω, "hold back, check". The two verbs differ by one letter, and either makes sense.

p: Sinaiticus and Venetus say the passions are "beaten back"; Swete prints "bent back".

readings.w: Swete's text (Alexandrinus has ἀνακαμπτόμεθα, "we are bent back", which Swete corrects)
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text, which keeps Alexandrinus's verb and corrects only its ending. Liddell and Scott give "bend back" for ἀνακάμπτω and "drive back, beat back; check" for ἀνακόπτω. Two codices against one makes "beaten back" a strong rival, and it would match the "muzzled" that follows, which also comes from Sinaiticus and Venetus.

p: Venetus adds the next words of Genesis 49:7 in Greek: "for it was willful".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints and Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)
Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes
readings.orig: Ἐπικατάρατος ὁ θυμὸς αὐτῶν ὅτι αὐθάδης
readings.en: Cursed be their anger, for it was self-willed
readings.plain: "Their anger be cursed, for it was willful."

why: The shorter quotation has two codices. A copyist who knew the Greek of Genesis 49:7 ("cursed be their anger, for it was self-willed", as Swete prints it) could easily finish the line.

p: Alexandrinus uses the book's word for reason (logismos) for the objector's argument; Venetus has logos, "argument".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints
Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵc), who also supplied the words the first hand left out

why: The base text's word is the harder reading: a copyist would more likely change the odd "reasoning is laughable" to "the argument is laughable" than the other way around.
b: The first hand of Codex Sinaiticus left out everything from "rules" in 2:24 to "reason" in 3:1 (Swete gives the gap as κρατει ληθης ... εαυτου παθων ο λογισμος); a corrector wrote the missing words in, in a slightly different form.

t: Seleucus Nicanor, or son of Nicanor?
p: Venetus reads "Seleucus, son of Nicanor".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints and Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)
Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes

why: Neither name fits the king meant (Seleucus IV); the base text is followed and the error explained in the note.

t: The priests, or the old men?
p: Sinaiticus has "the old men" praying in the temple with the women and children.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints and Codex Venetus (V)
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes

why: Two codices against one. The two Greek words look alike (ἱερέων / γεραιῶν), and 2 Maccabees 3:15 has the priests praying.

a: three thousand six hundred sixty talents
p: The first hand of Sinaiticus wrote "one thousand" for "three thousand"; a later corrector changed it.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints; Codex Venetus (V); a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵc.b)
readings.en: three thousand six hundred sixty talents
readings.plain: three thousand six hundred sixty talents

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand (ℵ*), from Swete's footnote
readings.en: one thousand six hundred sixty talents
readings.plain: one thousand six hundred sixty talents

why: All the other witnesses have three thousand. Either sum is far above the 360 talents of 2 Maccabees 4:8.

a: made the nation give up its way of life
t: Changed their way of life, or sought them out?
p: Alexandrinus says Jason "sought out" the nation; Sinaiticus and Venetus say he made it change its way of life.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes
readings.en: he changed the nation's way of living
readings.plain: made the nation give up its way of life

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints

why: This is a departure from the base text. "Sought out the nation" gives no clear sense beside "changed its form of government", while "changed their way of life" matches 2 Maccabees 4:10, where Jason "moved his own people over to the Greek stamp". The two Greek words differ by a few letters.

a: Not only did Jason build a gymnasium on top of our homeland's citadel; he also put an end to the care of the temple.
t: Did he also end the temple's care?
p: Alexandrinus lacks the words "but also did away with"; Swete supplies them from Sinaiticus and Venetus.

readings.w: Swete's text, with Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Codex Venetus (V)
readings.orig: ἀλλὰ καὶ καταλῦσαι τὴν τοῦ ἱεροῦ κηδεμονίαν
readings.en: but also to put an end to the care of the temple
readings.plain: Not only did Jason build a gymnasium on top of our homeland's citadel; he also put an end to the care of the temple.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints (it leaves out ἀλλὰ καὶ καταλῦσαι)
readings.orig: γυμνάσιον κατασκευάσαι ... τὴν τοῦ ἱεροῦ κηδεμονίαν
readings.en: to build a gymnasium ... the care of the temple
readings.plain: Jason built a gymnasium on top of our homeland's citadel ... the care of the temple.

why: Without the missing words the sentence in Alexandrinus does not hold together ("not only ... the care of the temple"), so Swete corrects it from the other two codices, and the Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. Brenton's English marks the gap with brackets.

t: Loyalty, or keeping of the law?
p: Sinaiticus and Venetus say the king could not break the nation's "good order under the law" (eunomia).

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Brenton's English ("obedience to the law")
readings.en: good order, keeping of the law

why: Both readings make sense. The base text is followed: "goodwill" toward their own law and people is what the decrees tried to break. Eunomia appears at 3:20 ("they kept the law well"), which might have led a copyist to write it here too.

a: because of his age many of the tyrant's court knew him
t: Known for his age, or for his philosophy too?
p: Venetus adds that the court knew Eleazar "for his philosophy".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints and Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)
readings.orig: πολλοῖς τῶν περὶ τὸν τύραννον διὰ τὴν ἡλικίαν γνώριμος
readings.en: known to many of those around the tyrant because of his age
readings.plain: because of his age many of the tyrant's court knew him

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD), from Swete's footnotes
readings.orig: πολλοῖς τῶν περὶ τὸν τύραννον διὰ τὴν ἡλικίαν γνώριμος διὰ τὴν φιλοσοφίαν
readings.en: known ... because of his age, for his philosophy
readings.plain: because of his age, and for his philosophy, many of the tyrant's court knew him

why: The addition has only one witness, and it looks like an explanation drawn from 5:35 and 7:7, where Eleazar is praised as a philosopher.
b: Swete's footnote also shows that Codex Sinaiticus leaves out "a Hebrew" in this verse.

a: I will not run from you
p: Sinaiticus reads "I will not swear you off".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints
readings.plain: I will not run from you

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes
readings.en: nor will I swear you off
readings.plain: I will not swear you off

why: Swete prints Alexandrinus. Sinaiticus's word echoes 4:26, where the king forces people to "swear off" Judaism, and that echo may have drawn a copyist to it; Venetus is lost from 5:11 on and cannot decide.

p: Alexandrinus says the torturers admired Eleazar's "good fortune"; Sinaiticus has "courage".

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Brenton's English ("courage")
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints

why: This is a departure from the base text. A man being flogged is not admired for his good fortune; the words differ by one letter (ευτυχια / ευψυχια), and courage is what the scene shows (6:5, 9-10). Venetus is lost here.

t: On their account, or on their behalf?
p: Sinaiticus has hyper, "on their behalf", the word of the New Testament's "died for us", in Eleazar's prayer.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the text Swete prints
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's footnotes

why: The base text is followed. Sinaiticus also has ὑπέρ for περί at 5:38, where nothing theological is at stake, so the change here need not be a theological one either; but ὑπέρ makes the idea of a penalty paid in place of others plainer. Venetus is lost here.
b: The prayer means much the same with either word: the suffering is offered for the nation's sake. In the New Testament ὑπέρ is the word of "Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8) and "one man should die on behalf of the people" (John 11:50).
